newsitem.title: UK: British government faces tight vote on handgun ban.
newsitem.headline: British government faces tight vote on handgun ban.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major faces a tight parliamentary vote on Monday on plans for a limited ban on pistols drawn up after the massacre of 16 children and their teacher by a crazed gunman at a school in Scotland.

Major faces a rebellion from a handful of ruling Conservative members of parliament who back demands by opposition parties and families of the victims from the Scottish town for a total ban on handguns.

The government hopes for support from Northern Ireland MPs and is confident of squeezing through. But with an overall majority of just one in the 651-seat parliament, a highly embarrassing government defeat cannot be ruled out.

The government has argued its limited move, which would ban 80 percent of legal handguns but allow small-calibre pistols used for target shooting to be held under tight control at gun clubs, would provide the necessary protection for the public.

"We want to see whether it is possible to do that while preserving to some extent a legitimate activity, that has been part of the Olympic Games since 1896," interior minister Michael Howard said on Monday.
"We have to consider whether a total ban on handguns would actually drive some legitimate activities underground and diminish the protection which the public get."
The children and their teacher were killed last March at Dunblane Primary School in a hail of bullets by gunman Thomas Hamilton, who then shot himself dead.

The government has came under criticism for imposing strict party discipline -- which means rebels could face penalties if they vote against the government -- for Monday night's vote on pistol restrictions following the massacre. Many members of parliament say the vote covers a matter above politics.
Robert Hughes, one of four Conservatives who have tabled an amendment calling for an outright ban, said: "There's no question that the Commons would ban all handguns on a free vote.

"I think that's the sadness of the government's decision not to have one. It struck me right from the beginning that here was a matter that was not party political, that I had to form my own judgment and work out what I thought was right."
The husband of Gwen Mayor, the teacher killed at Dunblane, made an emotional appeal to members of parliament to agree an outright ban.

Rodney Mayor told the Sun newspaper: "To every MP, I say: Think of the person you love most dearly and then think of 17 families identifying the bullet-ridden bodies of their loved ones...and decide if we want to risk a tragedy like this again."
